paragraphs: In reviewing the defects of the existing Confederation, and showing that no government with less energy than the one now before the public can remedy them, we naturally had to consider several of that government's most important principles. But the ultimate object of these papers is to determine clearly and fully the merits of this Constitution and the wisdom of adopting it. Our plan cannot be complete, then, unless we survey the work of the Convention more critically and thoroughly. We must examine it from every side, compare all its parts, and calculate its probable effects. If this remaining task is to be carried out in a frame of mind that leads to a just and fair result, I must first indulge in some reflections that fairness itself suggests.

It is a misfortune inseparable from human affairs that public measures are seldom examined in the spirit of moderation that a just estimate of their real tendency to help or hinder the public good requires. That spirit is more likely to be weakened than strengthened by the very occasions that demand an unusual amount of it. Those whom experience has led to notice this will not be surprised that the act of the Convention has met, or has stirred up, attitudes unfriendly to a fair discussion and accurate judgment of its merits, on one side as much as on the other. After all, it recommends so many important changes and innovations, it can be viewed in so many lights and relations, and it touches the springs of so many passions and interests. In some people it has been all too plain from their own publications that they have examined the proposed Constitution not merely with a leaning toward censure but with a settled decision to condemn it. The language of others betrays the opposite decision, or bias, and this makes their opinions of little weight in the question too. In putting these two kinds of people on the same level as to the weight of their opinions, I do not mean to suggest that there may not be a real difference in the purity of their intentions. It is only just to say in favor of the second kind that our situation is universally admitted to be peculiarly critical, and to require absolutely that something be done for our relief. The man who has decided in advance to support what has actually been done may therefore have drawn his bias from the weight of these considerations, as well as from motives of a sinister kind. The man who has decided in advance to oppose it, on the other hand, can have been moved by no excusable motive at all. The intentions of the first may be upright, though they may equally be blameworthy. The aims of the last cannot be upright, and must be blameworthy. But the truth is that these papers are not addressed to people of either description. They ask for the attention only of those who combine a sincere zeal for the happiness of their country with a temperament favorable to judging fairly the means of promoting it.

People of this character will set about examining the plan the Convention submitted without any wish to find faults or to magnify them. They will see that it is only reasonable to remember that a faultless plan was not to be expected. Nor will they merely make allowance for the errors that the Convention, as a body of men, was liable to commit because of human fallibility. They will bear in mind that they themselves are only men too, and ought not to assume infallibility when they rejudge the fallible opinions of others.

They will see just as readily that, apart from these reasons for fairness, many allowances should be made for the difficulties inherent in the very nature of the task that was entrusted to the Convention.

The novelty of the undertaking strikes us at once. These papers have shown that the existing Confederation is founded on false principles, so that we must change this first foundation and with it the structure resting on it. They have shown that the other confederacies which could be consulted as precedents were spoiled by the same erroneous principles, and so can offer no light except that of beacons, which warn of the course to be avoided without pointing out the one to be followed. The most the Convention could do in such a situation was to avoid the errors that the past experience of other countries, and of our own, had revealed, and to provide a convenient way of correcting its own errors as future experience might uncover them.

One very important difficulty the Convention met must have been the task of combining the necessary stability and energy in government with unfailing attention to liberty and to the republican form. If they had not substantially accomplished this part of their task, they would have fulfilled very imperfectly the object of their appointment and the expectation of the public. Yet no one who does not wish to betray his ignorance of the subject will deny that it could not easily be accomplished. Energy in government is essential to security against external and internal danger, and to the prompt and beneficial execution of the laws, both of which enter into the very definition of good government. Stability in government is essential to national character and the advantages that go with it, and also to that repose and confidence in the minds of the people which are among the chief blessings of civil society. A changeable and irregular legislation is no more an evil in itself than it is odious to the people. It may be said with assurance that the people of this country, enlightened as they are about the nature of good government and concerned as the great body of them are in its effects, will never be satisfied until some remedy is applied to the vicissitudes and uncertainties that mark the State administrations. But when we compare these valuable ingredients with the vital principles of liberty, we see at once how hard it is to mix them in their due proportions. The spirit of republican liberty seems to demand, on one side, not only that all power be derived from the people but that those entrusted with it be kept dependent on the people by the short duration of their appointments. It seems to demand also that even during this short period the trust be placed not in a few hands but in a number of them. Stability, on the contrary, requires that the hands in which power is lodged remain the same for a length of time. Frequent elections will bring a frequent change of men, and a frequent change of men will bring a frequent change of measures. Energy in government, meanwhile, requires not only a certain duration of power but that it be exercised by a single hand.
How far the Convention may have succeeded in this part of its work will appear better on a closer view of it. From the brief look taken here, it must be clear that this part was an arduous one.

Equally arduous must have been the task of marking the proper line of partition between the authority of the general government and that of the State governments. Every man will be aware of this difficulty in proportion as he has been accustomed to contemplate and distinguish objects that are extensive and complicated in their nature. Even the faculties of the mind have never yet been distinguished and defined with satisfactory precision, for all the efforts of the most acute and metaphysical philosophers. Sense, perception, judgment, desire, volition, memory and imagination are found to be separated by such delicate shades and minute gradations that their boundaries have eluded the most subtle investigation, and remain a rich source of ingenious discussion and controversy. The boundaries between the great kingdoms of nature, and still more between the various provinces and lesser portions into which they are subdivided, illustrate the same important truth. The most sagacious and laborious naturalists have never yet succeeded in tracing with certainty the line that separates the district of vegetable life from the neighboring region of unorganized matter, or that marks where the first ends and the animal empire begins. There is still greater obscurity in the distinguishing characters by which the objects in each of these great departments of nature have been arranged and sorted.

When we pass from the works of nature to the institutions of man, our hopes and expectations from the efforts of human sagacity must be moderated still further. In nature all the outlines are perfectly accurate, and appear otherwise only because the eye that surveys them is imperfect. In human institutions the obscurity comes as much from the object itself as from the organ that contemplates it. Experience has taught us that no skill in the science of government has yet been able to distinguish and define with sufficient certainty its three great provinces, the legislative, the executive and the judiciary, or even the privileges and powers of the different legislative branches. Questions arise daily in practice that prove the obscurity reigning over these subjects, and that puzzle the greatest adepts in political science.

The experience of ages, with the continued and combined labors of the most enlightened legislatures and jurists, has been equally unsuccessful in describing the several objects and limits of different codes of law and different courts of justice. In Great Britain, where accuracy in such subjects has been pursued more industriously than anywhere else in the world, the precise extent of the common law, the statute law, the maritime law, the ecclesiastical law, the law of corporations and other local laws and customs still remains to be clearly and finally settled. The jurisdiction of her separate courts, general and local, of law, of equity, of admiralty and so on, is no less a source of frequent and intricate disputes, which sufficiently show how indeterminate the limits are that circumscribe them. All new laws, though drafted with the greatest technical skill and passed after the fullest and most mature deliberation, are considered more or less obscure and equivocal until a series of particular discussions and judgments has settled and fixed their meaning. Besides the obscurity that comes from the complexity of objects and the imperfection of the human faculties, the medium through which men's conceptions are conveyed to each other adds a fresh embarrassment. The use of words is to express ideas. Clarity therefore requires not only that the ideas be distinctly formed but that they be expressed in words distinctly and exclusively suited to them. But no language is so copious as to supply words and phrases for every complex idea, or so correct as not to include many words that equivocally denote different ideas. It must follow that, however accurately objects may be distinguished in themselves, and however accurately the distinction may be considered, the definition of them may be made inaccurate by the inaccuracy of the terms in which it is delivered. This unavoidable inaccuracy must be greater or less according to the complexity and novelty of the objects defined. Even when the Almighty himself condescends to address mankind in their own language, his meaning, luminous as it must be, is made dim and doubtful by the cloudy medium through which it is communicated.

Here, then, are three sources of vague and incorrect definitions: the indistinctness of the object, the imperfection of the organ of conception, and the inadequacy of the vehicle of ideas. Any one of them must produce some degree of obscurity. In drawing the boundary between federal and State jurisdictions, the Convention must have felt the full effect of all three.

To the difficulties already mentioned we may add the conflicting claims of the larger and smaller States. We cannot be wrong in supposing that the larger States would contend for a share in the government fully proportioned to their greater wealth and importance, and that the smaller would be no less tenacious of the equality they now enjoy. We may well suppose that neither side would give way entirely to the other, and so the struggle could end only in compromise. It is also extremely probable that, after the ratio of representation had been settled, this very compromise must have produced a fresh struggle between the same parties. Each would try to shape the organization of the government and the distribution of its powers so as to increase the importance of those branches in forming which it had obtained the greatest share of influence. There are features in the Constitution that bear out each of these suppositions. And so far as either of them is well founded, it shows that the Convention must have been compelled to sacrifice theoretical propriety to the force of outside considerations.

Nor could it have been only the large and small States that lined up against each other on various points. Other combinations, arising from differences of local position and policy, must have created further difficulties. Every State may be divided into different districts, and its citizens into different classes, which give birth to contending interests and local jealousies. In the same way the different parts of the United States are distinguished from each other by a variety of circumstances that produce a like effect on a larger scale. And although this variety of interests may have a beneficial influence on the administration of the government once it is formed, for reasons sufficiently explained in an earlier paper, everyone must be aware of the opposite influence that was felt in the task of forming it.

Would it be surprising if, under the pressure of all these difficulties, the Convention had been forced into some departures from that artificial structure and regular symmetry which an abstract view of the subject might lead an ingenious theorist to give to a Constitution planned in his study or in his imagination? The real wonder is that so many difficulties were overcome, and overcome with a unanimity almost as unprecedented as it must have been unexpected. No man of fairness can reflect on this circumstance without sharing the astonishment. No man of pious reflection can fail to see in it a finger of that Almighty hand which has so often and so signally been extended to our relief at the critical stages of the recent revolution.

In an earlier paper we had occasion to notice the repeated and unsuccessful attempts made in the United Netherlands to reform the baneful and notorious vices of their constitution. The history of almost all the great councils and consultations held among mankind to reconcile their discordant opinions, calm their mutual jealousies and adjust their respective interests is a history of factions, contentions and disappointments. It may be ranked among the darkest and most degraded pictures that show the infirmities and depravities of the human character. If a few scattered instances present a brighter aspect, they serve only as exceptions that remind us of the general truth, and by their luster they deepen the gloom of the opposite prospect with which they are contrasted. When we consider the causes of these exceptions and apply them to the particular instance before us, we are necessarily led to two important conclusions. The first is that the Convention must have enjoyed, to a very singular degree, freedom from the pestilential influence of party animosities, the disease most common to deliberative bodies and most likely to contaminate their proceedings. The second conclusion is that all the deputations that made up the Convention were either satisfactorily accommodated by the final act or were brought to agree to it by a deep conviction of the necessity of sacrificing private opinions and partial interests to the public good, and by despair of seeing this necessity lessened by delay or by new experiments.
